source_caption:
To capture one of the most soaring, idyllic opening shots in cinematic history, the production had to subject Julie Andrews to surprisingly brutal physical conditions. While Maria flawlessly spins through the lush Austrian Alps singing the title track, the sweeping aerial footage was captured by a helicopter flying dangerously close to the ground. The immense, violently powerful downdraft from the chopper’s rotors repeatedly blasted Andrews face-first into the mud the very second she finished her joyful twirls. By masking this chaotic, exhausting physical endurance test behind a transcendent, radiant smile, she brilliantly physicalized the film’s core theme: finding unwavering, defiant joy even in the face of overwhelming turbulence.
⠀
The Sound of Music (1965), directed by Robert Wise, starring Julie Andrews, Christopher Plummer. A spirited young postulant leaves her Austrian convent to become a governess for a strict naval captain’s seven mischievous children, ultimately bringing music and life back into their home just as the terrifying shadow of the Third Reich threatens to consume their country.

source_details.title: The Sound of Music
source_details.synopsis: The Sound of Music is a 1965 American musical drama film produced and directed by Robert Wise from a screenplay written by Ernest Lehman. It is based on the 1959 stage musical composed by Richard Rodgers, with lyrics by Oscar Hammerstein II and a book by Lindsay and Crouse, itself based on the 1949 memoir The Story of the Trapp Family Singers by Maria von Trapp. The film stars Julie Andrews and Christopher Plummer, with Richard Haydn, Peggy Wood, Charmian Carr, and Eleanor Parker.
